PROJECT DESCRIPTION:
The project is being called “The Place @ Tweedy.” It is envisioned as a vibrant, community-
oriented food and entertainment destination designed to activate Tweedy Blvd throughout the day
and evening. The project integrates diverse culinary offerings, family-friendly amenities, and
curated live entertainment to create a cohesive and well-managed gathering space that contributes
to the revitalization of the Tweedy corridor. The applicant has referenced BLVD MRKT, a curated
food hall in Montebello, as an inspiration for this project in its ability to bring community together
around unique food options. BLVD MRKT was once an empty storefront and now serves as a
catalyst for new businesses along Whittier Boulevard.

Tenant Composition
The project includes four buildings, including a two-story building, a smaller building along
Tweedy Boulevard intended as a coffee shop, and a building located in the center of the property
along the eastern property line. There will be a total of eight (8) vendor spaces across two levels:

  •  Upper Level (1 Unit - 265 SQ.FT):
  o Terrace: The upper level will serve as an open-air terrace with a dedicated bar
  offering cocktails, beer, and wine. Guests seated on the terrace will enjoy a relaxed
  social atmosphere with shaded seating and views of the courtyard below.
   Food for terrace patrons will be prepared by the ground-level vendors and
  delivered directly to their tables through an “in-seat service” model.
   Guests will be able to browse menus and place orders via QR codes located
  at each table, allowing seamless coordination between the terrace and food
  vendors below.

  •  Ground Level (7 Units):
  o Six (6) Food Vendors:
   Coffee Shop (265 SQ.FT)
   Pizza Spot (365 SQ.FT)
   Burger Spot (365 SQ.FT)
   Taco Spot (365 SQ.FT)
   Churro/Dessert Spot (265 SQ.FT)
   Asian Fusion Spot (365 SQ.FT)

  o Bar (1 Unit - 265 SQ.FT):
   A ground-floor bar situated adjacent to the live entertainment area, serving
  beer, wine, and select mixed beverages for on-site consumption.

In addition to the vendor spaces, the project includes a dedicated children’s play area and an
outdoor performance space for small-scale live music and community events.

Hours of Operation
The collective hours of operation for the project are as follows:
  • General Hours: 10:00 AM – 11:00 PM, seven days a week
  • Coffee Shop: 7:00 AM – 4:00 PM
  • Expected peak hours:
  o Lunch: 11:00 AM – 2:00 PM
  o Dinner: 6:00 PM – 9:00 PM

These hours were selected to ensure a balanced flow of visitors throughout the day, encouraging
staggered parking demand and manageable peak-hour activity.

Alcohol Sales
Alcohol sales will occur in two dedicated bar areas—one located on the upper lounge level and
one on the ground floor near the entertainment area. Both will operate under the appropriate ABC
on-site consumption licenses. Alcohol will be served and consumed only within designated areas,
and no off-site alcohol consumption will be permitted. The project management team will oversee
responsible beverage service and compliance with all state and city regulations.

Live Entertainment
Live entertainment will be limited to musical performances of no more than four (4) performers at
a time. Performances will take place in the outdoor stage area adjacent to the ground-floor bar.

  Schedule of Entertainment:
  • Days: Friday, Saturday, and Sunday
  • Times: 12:00 PM – 10:00 PM

Entertainment will be oriented inward toward the courtyard to minimize sound transmission to
surrounding properties. All performances will comply with city noise standards and operational
conditions.

Sound System
A low-intensity distributed speaker system will be installed throughout the outdoor courtyard and
interior lounge areas to provide background music and limited sound reinforcement for live
entertainment. Speakers will be wall-mounted and directed inward to control sound projection.

Family and Community Amenities
The project includes a dedicated children’s play area designed as a safe and engaging environment
for families, encouraging broader community use. The project promotes inclusivity by combining
family-friendly programming with diverse dining options and social spaces.

Parking Management
Parking demand will be distributed across tenants based on operating hours and turnover rates.
The early closure of the coffee shop will allow for parking turnover in the afternoon and evening
when other food vendors experience higher traffic.

If necessary, the applicant is willing to coordinate with the City to designate 15-minute on-street
parking spaces during morning hours (7:00 AM–4:00 PM) to accommodate coffee shop customers.

Additionally, the applicant is exploring shared parking opportunities with neighboring properties
to further accommodate peak demand.

Operations and Management
The project will maintain a unified management team responsible for:
  • Overseeing daily operations, maintenance, and cleanliness of shared areas.
  • Coordinating deliveries during non-peak hours.
  • Enforcing vendor compliance with City-approved operational and noise regulations.
  • Managing trash collection schedules to minimize impact on adjacent uses.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS:

Under the California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
seq., “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 California Code of Regulations §§
15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”), the project qualifies as a Class 32 Categorical Exemption
pursuant to Section 15332 (Class 32 – Infill Development Projects) of the CEQA Guidelines (Title
14, Chapter 3 of the California Code of Regulations).

BACKGROUND:

Site History and Environmental Setting
The project site consists of three lots: one developed lot and two vacant lots. The developed lot
(3703 Tweedy Boulevard) at the northeastern corner of Tweedy Boulevard and San Carlos Avenue
has a one-story, 2,392 SF commercial building constructed in the 1950s. It was formerly used as a
dental/medical office, but the building is now vacant. Based on aerial photographs, the two vacant
lots located east of the commercial building have been vacant for over 30 years. There are no
building permits on file showing that the lots were ever developed.

The entire site is flat with paved sidewalks, stable valley soils, and surrounded by low-rise
commercial storefronts and nearby residences. Vegetation is minimal, limited to a few street trees
along the public sidewalks and ornamental plants onsite. There are no sensitive habitats or
protected species in the area. Wildlife consists of common urban birds and small mammals. There
are no known historical, cultural, or scenic designations on the property.

The property is part of the Tweedy Mile corridor and is required to have an active retail frontage
that encourages pedestrian activity. Properties along Tweedy Boulevard adjacent to the subject site
are developed with commercial uses. Residential uses are located to the north along San Carlos
Avenue.

History of Land Use and Zoning of Subject Property
In 1950, the property at 3703 Tweedy Boulevard was developed as a medical building. A 14-foot
by 28-foot carport was built in the rear of the building. There are no permits for the two vacant
lots to the east; however, a history of code violations has occurred over the decades, including
overgrown vegetation, weeds, trash, debris, and parking on an unimproved area. Violations of
graffiti have also been reported on the existing building.

In 2019, the City adopted the Tweedy Boulevard Specific Plan. The zoning for the subject property
and adjacent properties along Tweedy Boulevard was changed from Restricted Commercial (C-2)
to Tweedy Mixed Use-2 (TMU2). Properties to the west across San Carlos Avenue were changed
to Tweedy Mixed Use-1 (TMU1). An “Active Retail Frontage” corridor was established from
Elizabeth Avenue to the west to Bowman Avenue to the east, which includes the subject property.

  It should be noted that a CUP is also required for live entertainment, which is subject to review
  and approval by the City Council. The City Council will consider the proposed live entertainment
  at its regularly scheduled meeting on October 28, 2025.

  Required Findings for a CUP: Pursuant to SGMC Section 11.52.030, before a CUP may be
  granted, the Planning Commission (or the City Council on appeal) shall make all the following
  findings, as applicable to the property:

  A. Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose

  B. The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with
  the existing and future land uses of the applicable zone.

  C. Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to
  the character or function of the neighborhood.

  The proposed Resolution supports the findings required under Section 11.52.030.

  Municipal Code Conditions of Approval for Alcoholic Beverage Sales: Pursuant to SGMC Section

  Issues of Concern

  Parking
  The project site is within the Active Retail Frontage district commonly known as “Tweedy Mile.”
  Whereas the City’s Zoning Code provides for parking requirements based on land use types, the
  TBSP embraces the concept of shared parking, where parking supplies are available to all users,
  rather than being limited to a single land use or building (TBSP Chapter 5 – Mobility and Parking).
  The overall parking strategy for Tweedy Mile is to provide sufficient parking to ensure economic
  viability and success of commercial uses. The listed parking strategies in the TBSP include the
  “Park Once” concept and program, which “is intended to consolidate parking resources, relieve
  individual properties of providing potentially duplicative parking, reduce individual vehicle trips,
  and group parking facilities in strategically dispersed locations to encourage walking between
  destinations.”

  Per SGMC Section 11.33.040, a food use with 7,718 square feet of building area would be required
  to provide 115 onsite parking spaces. This is based on a factor of 40 spaces for the first 4,000
  square feet, plus 1 space for every 50 square feet over 4,000 square feet. However, per Assembly
  Bill 2097 (AB 2097) cities are prohibited from imposing a minimum automobile parking
  requirement on most development projects located within a half-mile radius of a major transit stop.
  Tweedy Boulevard is a major commercial and mixed-use corridor with adequate public transit.
  Furthermore, the TBSP encourages a walkable environment where visitors can visit multiple
  destinations and “park once.” This provides an opportunity for revised parking standards along
  Tweedy Mile. TBSP indicates there is a considerable amount of parking supply in the Specific
  Plan area, including 2,865 off-street parking spaces (78% privately owned; 22% owned by the
  City). Over 80% of the off-street supply, or 2,345 spaces, are located in Tweedy Mile where the
  project site is located. The off-street supply comprises 635 spaces in City-owned lots and 1,710
  spaces in private lots.

  In the Park Once Program Area, the parking requirements may be met within 1,300 feet (¼ mile)
  of a specific land use. The applicant has demonstrated in Attachment 2 that there are 144 public
  parking spaces within 0.15 miles of the project site. This does not include on-street parking and
  private parking lots. The public parking available on City-owned lots and public streets is more
  than adequate to meet the parking spaces otherwise required by Code. Furthermore, as mentioned
  earlier, the applicant is exploring opportunities with nearby properties for shared parking on
  private parking lots. A shared parking agreement would prevent towing of vehicles belonging to
  food hall customers if parked on a private lot in the event the owner of the private lot decides to
  enforce parking rules.

  Noise
  The proposed project includes live entertainment, which is subject to review and approval by the
  City Council. The City Council will consider the proposed live entertainment at its regularly
  scheduled meeting on October 28, 2025. Those most impacted are the residents north of the project
  site along San Carlos Avenue. Although there is an alley and public parking lot between the project
  site and adjacent residences, the closest distance is only about 60 feet building to building. A noise
  study has been prepared for City Council’s consideration and is included as an attachment.
  Conditions of approval have been included in the Resolution to mitigate noise impacts, which are
  based on the noise study’s recommendations. The conditions require the following:

  •  Reduced volume for speakers located in the rear terrace and upper lounge.
  •  Noise barriers:
  • 10-foot-high barrier for entrance along rear alley
  • 10-foot-high barrier in rear lounge
  • 7-foot-high barrier for play area
  •  Noise restrictions after 10 p.m. in rear areas
  •  Additional measures to ensure reduced noise impacts during operation

  City Council will consider impacts generated by live entertainment on October 28, 2025. This may
  include noise, parking, littering, and other issues.

2. NOISE

The magnitude by which noise affects its surrounding environment is measured on a
logarithmic scale in decibels (dB). Because the human ear is limited to hearing a specific
range of frequencies, the A-weighted filter system is used to form relevant results. A-
weighted sound levels are represented as dBA. Figure 3 shows typical A-weighted
exterior and interior noise levels that occur in human environments.

Several noise metrics have been developed to evaluate noise. L eq is the energy average
noise level and corresponds to a steady-state sound level that has the same acoustical
energy as the sum of all the time varying noise events. L max is the maximum noise level
measured during a sampling period, and Lxx are the statistical noise levels that are
exceeded xx-% of the time of the measurement. L 50 is the average noise level that is
exceeded 50% of the time, 30 minutes in a 60 minute period.

5. NOISE ANALYSIS

AGI acoustical data and advanced acoustic modeling technologies were used to evaluate
and assess the Project’s operations to determine if noise control measures will be
needed. The CadnaA Noise Prediction Model was used to estimate the worst-case
operations associated with the project. CadnaA uses industry-accepted propagation
algorithms and user defined sound power based on ISO 9613-2 standards. ISO 9613-2
is an internationally recognized standard that establishes a method for calculating the
attenuation of noise from outdoor propagation, in order to predict the levels of noise at a
distance from a variety of sources. The calculations account for classical sound wave
divergence, plus attenuation factors resulting from air absorption, basic ground effects,
and barrier/structure shielding. Air absorption was considered to be under “standard day”
conditions of 59° F and 70% relative humidity. The site plans and topography were
inputted into CadnaA to establish the x, y, and z site geometrics for the analysis. The
noise generated by future operations was calculated by inputting acoustical sources (AGI
in-house acoustical database of children playing, live music, background music, and
entertainment areas calibrated to number of occupants) as area sources with constant
level of activity. Refer to previous Figure 4 for the location of the analyzed noise sensitive
receptors (ST1 through ST3).

11.34.100 Violations and enforcement.
The NCO shall have primary responsibility, with such assistance of the police department as may be necessary
or desirable, for the enforcement of this chapter. The NCO may seek voluntary compliance by way of warning,
notice, or informational materials.

A.  Violations. Written notice shall be provided to the responsible party upon an initial violation of the provisions
of this chapter. Notice shall specify the time frame for violation correction, if applicable, or time frame for
permit/variance application submittal. No further action shall be taken where violations are voluntarily remedied
prior to or after written violation notice.

  3.  If the gathering is not voluntarily dispersed and additional city personnel and/or law enforcement

  i.  The actual cost to the city for law enforcement services, excluding the initial response provided by

  ii.  Damage to public property resulting from such law enforcement response.

  iii.  Injuries to any NCO or law enforcement personnel involved in such law enforcement response.

11.34.110 Noise variance.
The owner or operator of a noise source that violates any of the provisions of this chapter may file a variance
application, consistent with the procedures of Chapter 11.51, Permits and Procedures.

A variance application shall detail the approved method of achieving maximum compliance and a time schedule
for its accomplishment. In its determinations, the NCO shall consider the following:

  1.  The magnitude of nuisance caused by the offensive noise.

  2.  The uses of property within the area of impingement by the noise.

  3.  The time factors related to study, design, financing, and construction of remedial work.

  4.  The economic factors related to age and useful life of the equipment.

  5.  The general public interest, welfare, and safety.
